## Voice and idiolect

### Name the Level Before the Line

**Also called:** the dialogue selector, level before line, what are you actually fixing
**What it is:** The card at the head of the `dial.` shelf. It does not write a line. It asks the three questions this shelf's own pair graph asks over and over — **what are you fixing, who has to be holding something already, and what is this technique made of** — and hands back a named shortlist for each answer. The axes were not invented: they were read off the sixty-one `Yields to:` conditions the cards carry and the nine no-pair rows in `PAIR-AUDIT.md`, and the conditions that repeated became the questions. Every card cited here is cited by id.
**Effect on the audience:** None. This card is never spoken. It exists so that the line that is spoken was chosen against the scene, the audience's memory and the delivery format, rather than reached for because it is the move the writer most enjoys writing.
**Used for and where it works best:** Answer the three questions **in order and out loud, one sentence each, before you open either file**. Question one is the gate, and it is asked first because every condition that leaves this shelf leaves on it — the eight outward edges all say *the fix belongs at another level*. Questions two and three leave a shortlist of three to six. If you cannot answer question one, the scene is not broken at the line; rewrite the scene, not the dialogue. Where two answers fight over one exchange, that is two techniques, and one of them belongs in the next scene.
**Best in:** formats: all | genres: all
**Avoid when:** **The scene would still fail with perfect lines.** This map always returns a plausible card, including for a scene that should not exist, and a good technique laid over a dead scene reads as a writer with tools and nothing to say. Also **do not build a joke here**: six of the comedy cards on this shelf name a `comedy.` twin inside their own text — `comedy.literal_answer`, `comedy.non_sequitur`, `comedy.rule_of_three`, `comedy.funny_word_last`, `comedy.explained_joke`, `comedy.translation_resistance` — and the shape of the joke is settled there, while this shelf settles only whose mouth it comes out of. And **distrust axis one whenever your honest answer is its second value.** Two in every five reachable cards live under *the answer*, so on an ordinary two-hander the first question has barely narrowed anything and the whole load falls on axes two and three.
**Example:**
> **The scene:** a mother and her adult son, the diagnosis not yet said aloud. Ninety seconds, vertical, burned Arabic subtitles.
> **One — what am I fixing?** The answer. Not this person's permanent voice, not the shape of the scene.
> **Two — who has to be holding something?** The audience, and it is a fact: they already know the diagnosis.
> **Three — what is it made of?** It has to survive a subtitle, so not the words.
> **The shortlist:** `dial.half_truth` · `dial.known_information` · `dial.topic_change`.

**Prompt:** `[Selector — produces no prompt. It returns card ids. The chosen card carries the prompt.]`

---

**The axes**

**Axis 1 — What are you fixing: the person, the answer, the scene, or the connection?**
Asked first, because it is the only condition on which cards leave this shelf at all. **All eight outward edges are a level correction and nothing else:** `dial.conditional_tic` → `char.stress_tell` (*"The physical version; a character rarely has both"*), `dial.register_shift` → `rel.register_change` (*"The shift spans a relationship, not one scene"*), `dial.job_syntax` → `voice.dialect_by_syntax` (*"The marker is region, not occupation"*), `dial.second_language_rhythm` → `voice.second_language_voice` (*"The narrating version, not a spoken line"*), `dial.enter_late_leave_early` → `scene.arrival_scene` (*"The arrival itself is the scene"*), `dial.three_hander` → `scene.two_hander` (*"The third has nothing to want"*), `dial.table_scene` → `rel.pair_off_the_room` (*"Cast above seven and still unknown"*), `dial.confession_speech` → `info.reveal_lands_on_character` (*"Audience already knows it; play the listener"*). Nine conditions inside the shelf say the same thing to cards that stay — *"Nervous or lying characters over-complete, never clip"*, *"Other sociologies: take the mechanism, not the music"*, *"Arabic and similar: shift the naming register instead"*, *"Give each character a different sentence shape"*.

**Axis 2 — Who has to be holding something already, and is it a fact or a habit?**
This is the shelf's most repeated `Avoid when:` and it is stated as a fact every time, never as a feeling: *"The audience does not know what is being withheld"* (`dial.strategic_withholding`), *"The audience does not yet hold the missing fact"* (`dial.half_truth`), *"The audience does not yet know what is buried"* (`dial.topic_change`), *"Establish the terms plainly before anyone can reject them"* (`dial.refusing_the_frame`), *"The audience has not heard the baseline"* (`dial.register_shift`), *"The audience has only met the character under stress"* (`dial.fluency_under_stress`), *"Plant it three times in safe scenes before you use it as a tell"* (`dial.conditional_tic`), *"The audience already knows everything in it"* (`dial.confession_speech`), *"Cast above about seven and the audience does not yet know them"* (`dial.table_scene`). Its fourth value is the one the shelf never says out loud, and it is the largest: a technique that lands on first contact, owing nothing to any earlier page.

**Axis 3 — What is this technique actually made of: the words, the picture, the runtime, or the order?**
Seventeen conditions turn on survival rather than on effect, and they are the only conditions on this shelf that name a deliverable: *"Subtitled or burned-in work cannot carry simultaneity"* (`dial.overlap`), *"Subtitled or dubbed work flattens argot; syntax survives"* (`dial.argot_dose`), *"Vocabulary gets noticed, or must survive translation"* (`dial.signature_vocabulary`), *"Audio-only: listener loses who is speaking"* (`dial.interruption`), *"Audio: a silent character must be referred to aloud"* (`dial.who_is_silent`), *"Audio-only: a half-call is indistinguishable from monologue"* (`dial.one_sided_call`), *"Short formats cannot hold a played silence"* (`dial.silence_as_reply`), *"Short-form has no runtime for a surface"* (`dial.trivial_surface`), *"The scene is on a clock"* (`dial.interpreter_scene`), *"Localisation cost, or the scene must be warm"* (`dial.text_on_screen`). It is asked last because it is the only axis that reaches the telephone and bilingual regions at all, and because it closes an answer rather than opening one: on burned-subtitle work, one of its four values is shut before the writer starts.

**The default, and the one against it**

**The default is `dial.job_syntax`, and it is measured, not asserted.** It is the most-yielded-to card on the shelf: five cards send a reader to it, and nothing else on the shelf is named more than three times. `dial.clipped_line` sends you there (*"Other sociologies: take the mechanism, not the music"*), `dial.signature_vocabulary` sends you there (*"Vocabulary gets noticed, or must survive translation"*), `dial.argot_dose` sends you there (*"Subtitled or dubbed work flattens argot; syntax survives"*) — and so do **both** of the shelf's voice failures, `dial.phonetic_accent_spelling` (*"Accent belongs in word order, never in spelling"*) and `dial.writer_voice_uniformity` (*"Give each character a different sentence shape"*). The shelf, asked sixty-one times where to fall back to, falls back here more than anywhere else, and it falls back here from its own worst outcomes. It is also the only card that answers *the order* on axis three and *nobody* on axis two at the same time: it costs no plant, survives translation, survives audio, survives ninety seconds. That is why it is the default, and it is also why it is dull — the shelf reaches for it whenever something more interesting has failed.

**The one against it is `dial.lag_as_drama`.** Nothing routes to it, it is named by no `Yields to:` anywhere on the shelf, and `PAIR-AUDIT.md` files it with no alternative at all. Every other card here assumes the other person hears you now: the exchange cards fight over what a reply does, the group cards fight over who gets to reply, the telephone cards move the reply to another room. This one puts the drama in the **interval** — the answer arrives after it could have helped, and neither character did anything wrong. Its stated cost is precise and payable: under about two seconds the audience blames the sound mix, so the gap must be long and established early, which costs one harmless exchange. Its near cousin against the grain is `dial.three_hander`, likewise never yielded to by anything, and whose own card calls it *the most under-used scene shape in dialogue* — a claim this shelf's own graph confirms, since two in every three reachable cards are written for two people in a room.

**The pair graph of this shelf is a graph of the two-hander.** A writer working two people in a room is offered an alternative at every card; a writer who needs a third person, a floor, a telephone or a laugh is never sent there by anything and has to already know the region exists. The sixty-one readers who wrote these fields were each holding one exchange, and an exchange has two people in it. **That is why axis one is asked first, and why it is asked as *what are you fixing* rather than *what does this line do*** — the second phrasing would have reproduced the graph's own blind spot.

The second thing the list shows: **the whole mediated block sits in it.** `dial.text_on_screen`, `dial.video_call` and `dial.lag_as_drama` are unasked, and `dial.voice_note` is filed `pointer-only` in `PAIR-AUDIT.md` — it has no alternative because there is nothing standing next to it. So the shelf's one genuine gap is not a technique, it is an interlocutor: **nothing here covers a line spoken to someone who is not a person and cannot answer** — the prayer, the letter read aloud, the words said to the dead, the words said to a machine. The file's own coverage note lists exactly that as still to write, and the nearest thing that exists, `dial.voice_note`, already records the mechanism (*the format supplies the reason nobody speaks back*) without anything routing a reader there to find it.

### Signature Vocabulary

**Also called:** the lexical fingerprint, the word only they use
**What it is:** One character owns two or three words or constructions that no other character in the work is permitted to use. Not a catchphrase — ordinary words, consistently chosen where a synonym was available.
**Effect on the audience:** They can identify the speaker with the name covered. That recognition is felt as character depth even though it is really only consistency.
**Used for and where it works best:** Any cast above four, and mandatory in audio formats where there is no face to carry identity. Build it from the character's history, not their mood: a man who spent nine years in a warehouse says *shift*, *stock*, *short* where another says *time*, *stuff*, *missing*. The craft rule is exclusivity — the word does no work until you have taken it out of everyone else's mouth. Do the removal pass on the whole script, not on the character's scenes.
**Best in:** formats: Novel, One-Hour Drama, Audio Drama, Podcast, Stage Play, Limited Series, Animation Feature | genres: Drama, Family Drama, Crime, Social Drama, Heritage, Comedy
**Avoid when:** The word is distinctive enough to notice. A vocabulary the audience can name has become a tic and will be parodied by episode four. The test is that a reader can pick the speaker but cannot say why.
**Example:**
> **NABIL:** "It's fine. It'll hold."
> **SAMIRA:** "It's fine. It'll do for now."
>
> He repairs. She postpones. Neither ever uses the other's verb.

**Yields to:** `dial.job_syntax` — Vocabulary gets noticed, or must survive translation.  
`dial.signature_vocabulary`

### The Conditional Verbal Tic

**Also called:** the stress tic, the situational habit
**What it is:** A repeated verbal habit — a filler, a hedge, a throat-clear phrase, a name used, a question tag — that appears only under a specific condition, and disappears the rest of the time.
**Effect on the audience:** An early-warning system. Once the audience has learned the condition, the tic arriving in a calm scene tells them something is wrong before any line says so.
**Used for and where it works best:** Characters who conceal. Set the condition narrowly — *only when lying*, *only in front of his brother*, *only when he is about to refuse* — and plant it three times in safe scenes before you use it as a tell. It is the cheapest suspense mechanism in dialogue because the audience does the detecting. Pairs directly with `char.stress_tell`, which is the physical version; a character should rarely have both.
**Best in:** formats: One-Hour Drama, Novel, Limited Series, Feature Film, Audio Drama, Game Narrative | genres: Crime, Thriller, Psychological, Family Drama, Noir, Drama
**Avoid when:** The tic is unconditional. A constant *y'know* is transcription, not characterisation — it slows every line, survives no read-aloud, and is the first thing an actor asks to cut. If it appears in more than one scene in five, it has stopped being information.
**Example:**
> "Where were you?"
> "Work. Just work, that's all."
>
> *Three scenes earlier, telling the truth:* "Work."

**Yields to:** `char.stress_tell` — The physical version; a character rarely has both.  
`dial.conditional_tic`

### Register Shift

**Also called:** changing gear, the formality jump
**What it is:** A single character's level of formality moves inside a scene — from slang to correct grammar, from first names to titles, from dialect to standard — in response to who enters, what is asked, or what they have decided.
**Effect on the audience:** They read the social calculation instantly. A register shift is a character telling the room what they now think the room is.
**Used for and where it works best:** Anywhere a character crosses a social boundary: an interview, a police stop, a hospital, a visit home after years away. It is the most reliable way to dramatise class, migration and assimilation without stating any of it. The craft rule: shift on a specific trigger the audience can see, and let one shift per scene do the work. Where the shift is happening between two people over a whole relationship, `rel.register_change` is the larger version of the same move.
**Best in:** formats: Feature Film, One-Hour Drama, Novel, Stage Play, Limited Series, Short Film | genres: Social Drama, Family Drama, Drama, Coming of Age, Political, Heritage, Satire
**Avoid when:** The audience has not heard the baseline. A shift only exists against an established register, so a character introduced mid-shift reads as inconsistent rather than strategic. Give them one plain scene first.
**Example:**
> "Yeah, nah, he's my cousin's mate, it's nothing, we just —"
> *The officer takes out a pad.*
> "I have known him approximately two years. We are not close."

**Yields to:** `rel.register_change` — The shift spans a relationship, not one scene.  
`dial.register_shift`

### Syntax Carries the Job

**Also called:** occupational grammar, the trade in the sentence
**What it is:** A character's work shows in the *shape* of their sentences rather than in their vocabulary — the order they put things in, whether they lead with the conclusion or the evidence, whether they use the passive, how they handle uncertainty.
**Effect on the audience:** Authority without exposition. The audience believes the character does the job because the sentence is built the way that job builds sentences.
**Used for and where it works best:** The strongest character-voice tool there is, and the one that survives translation, which vocabulary does not. Nurses front the vital fact and hedge nothing. Lawyers qualify before they assert. Soldiers give the order then the reason. Engineers say what failed before who was there. Accountants use the passive to move blame off people. Write one line each way and keep the one whose *order* is wrong for everyone else in the scene. Cross-reference `voice.dialect_by_syntax` for the regional version of the same mechanism.
**Best in:** formats: all narrative | genres: Crime, Political, War, Social Drama, Drama, Thriller, Historical
**Avoid when:** You have not researched the job. Guessed syntax is worse than no syntax, because anyone in the trade hears it immediately and the character dies for that portion of the audience. One hour with a real practitioner buys more voice than a month of invention.
**Example:**
> **Nurse:** "BP's dropping, he's cold, I need you now."
> **Lawyer:** "Subject to what the file says, and I haven't seen the file, there may be an argument."
> **Contractor:** "Wall's wet. Been wet a while. Somebody painted over it."

**Yields to:** `voice.dialect_by_syntax` — The marker is region, not occupation.  
`dial.job_syntax`

### Professional Argot Dosing

**Also called:** the jargon ration, shop talk
**What it is:** Real trade terminology used at a deliberately controlled rate, with meaning carried by context and consequence rather than by explanation.
**Effect on the audience:** Immersion and the pleasure of eavesdropping. An audience will happily not understand a term if they can see what it does to the people in the room.
**Used for and where it works best:** Procedurals, workplace drama, heritage and historical work with a craft at its centre. The working ration is one unexplained term per exchange and never two in a line; the audience needs a comprehensible sentence on either side of it. Never define a term in dialogue between two people who both know it — that is `dial.known_information` from Part 1, and it kills the scene. If a term is genuinely load-bearing for the plot, buy the explanation with `dial.expert_explains_badly` instead. `expo.jargon_threshold` holds the wider budget rule.
**Best in:** formats: One-Hour Drama, Feature Film, Limited Series, Documentary, Podcast, Game Narrative, Novel | genres: Crime, Political, War, Historical, Heritage, Thriller, Social Drama
**Avoid when:** The work will be subtitled or dubbed into a language with no equivalent trade vocabulary. Argot is the first thing a subtitle flattens, and a scene built entirely on it arrives in the second language as generic. For subtitled projects, carry the world in `dial.job_syntax` instead, which survives.
**Example:**
> "Who signed the deposit sheet?"
> "Nobody. It came up out of context."
> "Then it's not evidence, it's a souvenir."

**Yields to:** `dial.job_syntax` — Subtitled or dubbed work flattens argot; syntax survives.  
`dial.argot_dose`

### Second-Language Rhythm

**Also called:** L2 voice, the fluent-thinking speaker
**What it is:** A character speaking a language that is not their first is written through grammar, idiom choice and sentence length — over-correct constructions, avoided idioms, the article dropped or added, the long way round a word they cannot retrieve — and never through misspelled pronunciation.
**Effect on the audience:** Respect for the character's intelligence. Done well, the audience hears a fluent mind working through a narrow channel, which is the actual experience; done badly they hear a simpleton.
**Used for and where it works best:** Migration stories, occupation and war, diaspora family drama, any scene where a character is more articulate in the room they are not in. Two rules make it work. First, the character is *more* formal, not less — learners acquire textbook register and keep it, so they say "I do not think so" where a native says "nah". Second, give them one moment of full fluency in their own language, heard or subtitled, so the audience knows what the channel is costing. Related: `voice.second_language_voice` for the narrating version.
**Best in:** formats: Feature Film, Novel, One-Hour Drama, Limited Series, Stage Play, Short Film, Documentary | genres: Social Drama, Family Drama, War, Drama, Coming of Age, Heritage, Political
**Avoid when:** The character's difficulty is being used for comedy you have not earned, or when the plot requires them to be quick — a scene of rapid verbal combat cannot be fought in a second language, and forcing it either makes the character implausibly fluent or the scene implausibly slow. Change the scene, not the character.
**Example:**
> "I am not able to explain it in a good way. In my language I could tell you this in one word."
> "Say it in your language."
> "It will not help you."

**Yields to:** `voice.second_language_voice` — The narrating version, not a spoken line.  
`dial.second_language_rhythm`

### Generational Speech Markers

**Also called:** age in the sentence, cohort idiom
**What it is:** Placing a character in a generation through the specific speech habits of that cohort — how they open a sentence, how they signal agreement, whether they use rising intonation, how they refer to technology, what they apologise for.
**Effect on the audience:** Instant demographic placement, and the friction between generations made audible rather than stated.
**Used for and where it works best:** Family drama across three generations, coming-of-age, workplace comedy with an age gap. The durable markers are structural, not lexical: older speakers finish sentences and expect the floor; younger speakers hedge assertions into questions and abandon sentences mid-clause; the middle cohort over-explains. Build on those, and use at most one current slang word per character as seasoning. For period work, the marker is what a generation is *embarrassed* by, which changes faster than its vocabulary.
**Best in:** formats: Half-Hour Comedy, One-Hour Drama, Novel, Feature Film, Vertical Micro-Drama, Reels/Shorts, Animation Feature | genres: Family Drama, Comedy, Coming of Age, Social Drama, Satire, Drama
**Avoid when:** The work needs a shelf life. Current slang dates a script faster than any other element — a line that reads as current in production reads as embarrassing at release eighteen months later, and unwatchable in syndication. If the project has a long tail, take the syntax and leave the vocabulary. This card is the most perishable in the file.
**Shelf life:** dated — review 2027-03. Current slang dates within about eighteen months. The craft underneath is durable: generation shows in syntax and reference, not in vocabulary.
**Example:**
> **Grandmother:** "You will call me when you arrive."
> **Mother:** "Just — a text is fine, honestly, whenever, I know you're busy, I just worry, that's all it is."
> **Daughter:** "Yeah no I'll—" *(she is already gone)*

`dial.generational_speech`

### Phonetic Accent Spelling

**Also called:** eye dialect, respelled accent
**This is a named failure, not a recommendation.**
**What it is:** Writing a character's accent by misspelling ordinary words to approximate their pronunciation — *dat*, *tink*, *vould*, *'appen* — while the other characters' identical sounds are spelled correctly.
**Effect on the audience:** Condescension they can feel. The respelled character reads as less intelligent, because misspelling is a signal of illiteracy in every other context a reader has met.
**Used for and where it works best:** Only one survival, and it is narrow: a single respelled word, once, where the mispronunciation is itself the plot — a name said wrong, a password mangled, an order misheard down a radio. One word, one time, and the respelling belongs to the moment rather than to the character.
**Best in:** formats: — | genres: —
**Avoid when:** Always, and note the asymmetry that proves the problem: no writer respells the accent of the character they identify with. Everyone has an accent; only the outsider gets misspelled. The replacements are better anyway — `dial.job_syntax` for word order, `dial.second_language_rhythm` for grammar, `voice.dialect_by_syntax` for region, and one line of action description telling the reader what the voice sounds like, which costs a sentence and works for the whole script.
**Example:**
> **Failure:** "Ah dinnae ken whit yer oan aboot, pal, an' Ah'm no' gonnae staun here an' —"
> **Working:** *Glasgow, and not softened for anyone.* "I don't know what you're on about. And I'm not standing here."

**Yields to:** `dial.job_syntax` — Accent belongs in word order, never in spelling.  
`dial.phonetic_accent_spelling`

### Everybody Talks Like the Writer

**Also called:** voice uniformity, the single-throat cast
**This is a named failure, not a recommendation.**
**What it is:** Every character shares one vocabulary, one sentence length, one sense of humour and one level of articulacy — the writer's. Names change; the voice does not.
**Effect on the audience:** Flatness they usually misdiagnose as a plot problem. The scenes feel talky and the cast feels thin, and neither more incident nor better structure repairs it.
**Used for and where it works best:** One place only, and it is a declared style rather than an accident: a stylised world where a uniform heightened register is the convention, as in some satire and most absurdist theatre. The test of whether it was a decision is consistency — a declared style applies to every character including the least sympathetic, and survives a read-aloud.
**Best in:** formats: — | genres: —
**Avoid when:** Everywhere else. The diagnostic is the swap test and it is merciless: cover the character names and read the scene: if any two lines could change mouths without changing meaning, the voices do not exist yet. Run it on every scene above two pages. The fix is never "add tics" — it is to give each character a different *sentence length* and a different relationship to certainty, then rewrite the scene once per character with only that character's lines in front of you.
**Example:**
> **Before:** "I think we need to consider what happens if this doesn't work out."  /  "I think we need to be realistic about the risks involved here."
> **After:** "And if it doesn't?"  /  "It will. I've run it twice."

**Yields to:** `dial.job_syntax` — Give each character a different sentence shape.  
`dial.writer_voice_uniformity`

---

## Comedy of dialogue

### The Literal Answer

**Also called:** answering the actual words, deliberate literalism
**What it is:** A character responds to the surface meaning of a rhetorical question, an idiom or a courtesy, as though it were a request for information.
**Effect on the audience:** The laugh of recognition — they heard the literal meaning too and suppressed it, and the character did not.
**Used for and where it works best:** Two very different characters own this move: the one who does not read social code, and the one who reads it perfectly and is refusing it. Both are funny, and the second is also aggressive, which makes it usable in drama. The craft rule is that the literal answer must be *correct*: the joke dies the moment the reply is merely silly rather than accurate. It also needs a straight partner who reacts, so build the pair before the joke. `comedy.literal_answer` holds the wider treatment of the mechanism outside dialogue.
**Best in:** formats: Half-Hour Comedy, Animation Feature, Feature Film, Stage Play, Reels/Shorts, Novel, Comics | genres: Comedy, Satire, Family Drama, Crime, Drama
**Avoid when:** The character is supposed to be warm and the scene is supposed to be moving. Literalism reads as withholding, and used at an emotional peak it makes the audience dislike the speaker in a way the script has not planned for.
**Example:**
> "Can I ask you something?"
> "You just did."
> "Can I ask you something else."
> "Now you've done it twice."

**Yields to:** `dial.undercut` — Warm scene: puncture yourself, not the other.  
`dial.literal_answer`

### Escalating Agreement

**Also called:** yes-and to destruction, over-agreeing
**What it is:** A character agrees with an accusation or a complaint, then agrees harder, then agrees past the point the accuser was prepared to go, until the accuser is defending the person they were attacking.
**Effect on the audience:** Delight at a reversal achieved with no resistance. The audience watches an argument lost by winning it.
**Used for and where it works best:** Guilt, apology and blame scenes, and anywhere a character is cornered and cannot deny. It is the comic sibling of `dial.concession_that_wins` in Part 1 — the drama version stops at one concession, this one keeps going until it tips. The rule: three steps, and the third must cost the speaker something real, or the audience reads it as sarcasm rather than escalation. Works in drama too, where the third step stops being funny; that switch is the most reliable tonal pivot in the technique.
**Best in:** formats: Half-Hour Comedy, Feature Film, Stage Play, One-Hour Drama, Podcast, Novel | genres: Comedy, Satire, Family Drama, Drama, Social Drama, Romance
**Avoid when:** The accuser is right and the scene needs them to stay right. Escalating agreement transfers sympathy to the agreeing character automatically, so deploying it defends whoever uses it — which is a problem if you were building a case against them.
**Example:**
> "You forgot."
> "I forgot."
> "You always forget."
> "I always forget. I forgot last year. I forgot the year your father was ill."
> "...Alright."
> "I'm not finished."

**Yields to:** `dial.concession_that_wins` — Drama: stop at one concession.  
`dial.escalating_agreement`

### The Non Sequitur Reply

**Also called:** the unconnected answer, the swerve to nowhere
**What it is:** A reply with no logical relation to the line before it, delivered with full conviction and never acknowledged as strange by the speaker.
**Effect on the audience:** Surprise, then the retrospective search for a connection — which is where most of the laugh actually lives. A non sequitur the audience can half-justify is funnier than one that is pure noise.
**Used for and where it works best:** Establishing a character's interior world in one line, and breaking a scene that has become too rational. It is also the fastest tone-setter in short-form: a reel has no time to build a comic character, but one non sequitur declares the whole register. The craft rule that separates it from randomness: the reply must be *consistent* with that character's obsession, so the second one lands harder than the first. `comedy.non_sequitur` covers the structural version.
**Best in:** formats: Half-Hour Comedy, Reels/Shorts, Animation Feature, Stage Play, Comics, Vertical Micro-Drama, Podcast | genres: Comedy, Satire, Drama
**Avoid when:** The scene is carrying plot. A non sequitur costs the audience one beat of comprehension, and in a scene where they are tracking information that beat is expensive. It also fails entirely in subtitled work if the connection is idiomatic — the subtitle strips the thread the audience was meant to half-find.
**Example:**
> "They're letting twelve people go on Friday."
> "My brother had a tortoise."
> "Hisham."
> "It lived forty years. Forty. On lettuce."

**Yields to:** `dial.deflating_reply` — The scene carries plot; a swerve costs comprehension.  
`dial.non_sequitur_reply`

### The Undercut

**Also called:** self-puncture, the deflating tag
**What it is:** A character delivers a serious, sincere or grand line and then immediately undermines it themselves, with a tag, a correction or an admission.
**Effect on the audience:** Affection. A character who punctures their own grandeur is one the audience trusts, because they have shown they can see themselves.
**Used for and where it works best:** Characters who must be admirable without being insufferable — leaders, mentors, romantic leads, anyone who has to make a speech. Used once at the end of a sincere passage it buys back all the earnestness the passage spent. The rule is placement: the undercut goes *after* the sincere line has landed with a beat of silence, never in the same breath, or the sincerity never registers and there is nothing to deflate.
**Best in:** formats: Feature Film, Half-Hour Comedy, One-Hour Drama, Novel, Stage Play, Limited Series | genres: Comedy, Romance, Drama, Coming of Age, Satire, Family Drama, War
**Avoid when:** The moment must stand. A script that undercuts every sincere line has told the audience that nothing in it can be meant, and the ending will not work — by then the audience is braced for the puncture. Ration it, and remove it entirely from the final ten minutes.
**Example:**
> "I've never been prouder of anything in my life than I am of this."
> *Beat.*
> "It's a shed."

**Yields to:** `dial.deflating_reply` — The puncture should come from someone else.  
`dial.undercut`

### The Comic Triple in Speech

**Also called:** the spoken rule of three, list-and-break
**What it is:** A character builds a list of three inside a single line or across three exchanges, where the first two items establish a category and the third breaks it.
**Effect on the audience:** The pattern-recognition pleasure of a joke they were invited to predict and then were wrong about. Three is the smallest number that makes a pattern, which is why two does not land and four is a speech.
**Used for and where it works best:** Any place a laugh must be reliable rather than inspired — this is the most dependable joke shape in existence and it works in every language. Two craft rules do all the work. The break must belong to the same category grammatically and a different one in meaning. And the funniest word goes last: reorder the line until the surprise is the final word, because a laugh cannot begin until the sentence ends. `comedy.rule_of_three` covers the structural version across scenes, and `comedy.funny_word_last` the placement rule.
**Best in:** formats: Half-Hour Comedy, Reels/Shorts, Feature Film, Stage Play, Podcast, Novel, Animation Feature | genres: Comedy, Satire, Family Drama, Romance, Coming of Age
**Avoid when:** The scene is already in a rhythm of threes. A triple inside a triple flattens both, and a script where every joke has this shape becomes audibly mechanical — an audience that starts counting has stopped laughing. It also cannot be used at speed in subtitled work: the reader is on item two when the actor reaches three.
**Example:**
> "He brought flowers, he apologised to my mother, and he asked if the car was still in my name."

**Yields to:** `dial.undercut` — Subtitled, or the scene already runs on threes.  
`dial.comic_triple`

### The Deflating Reply

**Also called:** the flat return, puncturing the other person
**What it is:** One character makes an emotional, dramatic or self-important statement and the other replies with something short, practical and entirely unimpressed.
**Effect on the audience:** Release. It gives permission to find the first character ridiculous, which the audience often already privately did.
**Used for and where it works best:** Double acts, long marriages, siblings, partners in a procedural. It is distinct from `dial.undercut`, where the speaker punctures themselves — here the puncture is an act by someone else, so it also carries relationship information. The rule: the deflating line must be shorter than the line it deflates, by a lot. Length is the whole mechanism; a witty reply of equal length is an exchange, not a deflation. It is also the correct tool for a scene that is sliding into melodrama and you do not want to cut.
**Best in:** formats: Half-Hour Comedy, One-Hour Drama, Feature Film, Stage Play, Vertical Micro-Drama, Novel, Audio Drama | genres: Comedy, Crime, Family Drama, Romance, Drama, Noir, Satire
**Avoid when:** The emotional statement is the one the whole script has been building toward. Deflating a genuine breakthrough does not create tonal balance, it cancels the scene, and audiences do not get that moment offered twice. Also avoid giving it to the same character every time, which turns them from dry into cruel across an episode without anyone deciding that.
**Example:**
> "I have given this family twenty-six years. Twenty-six years of my life."
> "Eat something."

**Yields to:** `dial.silence_as_reply` — The emotional line is the script's real breakthrough.  
`dial.deflating_reply`

### Talking Past the Laugh

**Also called:** stepping on the joke, the trailing tag
**This is a named failure, not a recommendation.**
**What it is:** The funny word or image arrives, and then the line — or the next line — keeps going, explaining, softening or repeating it, so that the laugh has nowhere to happen.
**Effect on the audience:** Nothing. Which is the point: the joke was present and did not fire, and neither the writer nor the room can usually tell why.
**Used for and where it works best:** Nowhere as a choice. It has no legitimate version — unlike most defects in this file, there is no stylised context in which stepping on your own joke is the convention.
**Best in:** formats: — | genres: —
**Avoid when:** Always, and it is a rewriting failure rather than a writing one — almost every first draft has it, because the writer is still finding the joke while typing. Three fixes, in order. Cut everything after the funny word in the line. Cut the first half of the *next* line, which is usually a reaction that explains. And in performance formats, put a beat of action after the joke so the laugh has physical room; on the page in prose, end the paragraph there. Related: `comedy.explained_joke`, which is the same disease at scene scale.
**Example:**
> **Failure:** "It's a shed, and I know it's just a shed, but you have to understand what it means to me after everything."
> **Working:** "It's a shed."

**Yields to:** `dial.action_beat` — Give the laugh physical room instead of words.  
`dial.talking_past_the_laugh`

---

## Monologue craft

### The Earned Speech

**Also called:** permission to speak at length, the paid-for monologue
**What it is:** A single character holding the floor for a sustained stretch, positioned so that the audience *wants* them to and the other characters cannot stop them. The craft is entirely in what the script does before the speech, not in the speech.
**Effect on the audience:** Release of accumulated pressure. A speech is a dam breaking; if there was no dam, it is just water.
**Used for and where it works best:** Once per feature, once or twice per series, and the position is close to fixed: after the character has been denied the floor repeatedly, or after they have deflected for an hour. Three conditions buy the permission. The character must have been interrupted, silenced or evasive before. There must be a reason they can speak *now* and could not before. And someone in the scene must need to hear it. If all three are present the audience will sit for three pages; if one is missing they will not sit for one.
**Best in:** formats: Stage Play, Feature Film, One-Hour Drama, Limited Series, Novel, Audio Drama | genres: Drama, Tragedy, Family Drama, Social Drama, Political, War, Coming of Age
**Avoid when:** It is the character's introduction, or the audience does not yet know what the speech is about. An unearned monologue is the single most common reason a good script is put down at page twelve. Also avoid in vertical micro-drama and reels, which have no runtime to build the dam.
**Example:**
> **Scenes 3, 9, 14:** every time he starts, someone answers the phone, or leaves, or says "not now".
> **Scene 27:** *He puts the phone in the drawer. He closes the drawer.*
> "Sit down. All of you sit down."

**Yields to:** `dial.voice_note` — Short-form or unearned floor; the form grants permission.  
`dial.earned_speech`

### The Interrupted Monologue

**Also called:** the broken speech, reactive monologue
**What it is:** A long speech deliberately broken by short lines, physical action or attempts to stop it, so that the speech is a scene with two people in it rather than a block of text with one.
**Effect on the audience:** They stay. An uninterrupted page of speech is skimmed; the same content broken four times is read, because each interruption resets attention and confirms that somebody in the room is still there.
**Used for and where it works best:** Screen formats above all, where a monologue longer than about half a page stops reading as dialogue and starts reading as narration, unless the script has earned the speech under the conditions `dial.earned_speech` sets. Break it where the listener's resistance is highest, not at convenient pauses — the interruption should be an attempt to escape the speech. The strongest version has the interruptions get shorter as the speech goes on, until the listener has nothing left, which stages the defeat instead of describing it.
**Best in:** formats: Feature Film, One-Hour Drama, Limited Series, Half-Hour Comedy, Short Film, Animation Feature | genres: Drama, Family Drama, Crime, Political, Social Drama, Tragedy, Comedy
**Avoid when:** The form is the point and the form is unbroken — a soliloquy on stage, a courtroom summation, a piece to camera in a documentary. Breaking those is not craft, it is a failure of nerve about a convention the audience already accepts.
**Example:**
> "You want to know what I did with it. I'll tell you what I did with it—"
> "I don't—"
> "—I paid the man on Rashid Street, and I paid your brother's fine, and I paid for the stone—"
> "Stop."
> "—the stone with her name on it that you have never once gone to see."

**Yields to:** `dial.earned_speech` — Soliloquy, summation, piece to camera: unbroken by convention.  
`dial.interrupted_monologue`

### The Confession Speech

**Also called:** the admission, telling it at last
**What it is:** A character says aloud, at length, the thing the story has been organised around concealing.
**Effect on the audience:** The largest single payoff available in dialogue, and the most easily wasted. The audience has been paying into it for the whole work.
**Used for and where it works best:** Late, and once. Four rules govern it and they are not optional. The confession must contain one fact the audience did not have, or it is only a summary. It must be told to the person it costs most to tell, not to a priest, a stranger or the camera. It must be told badly — out of order, with self-justification in it, with the worst part arriving last and accidentally. And it must change what the listener does, immediately. A confession that alters nothing is a scene the script did not need. Related: `info.reveal_lands_on_character`.
**Best in:** formats: Feature Film, Stage Play, One-Hour Drama, Novel, Limited Series, Audio Drama | genres: Crime, Drama, Tragedy, Family Drama, Psychological, Noir, War
**Avoid when:** The audience already knows everything in it. Then it is not a confession, it is the character catching up with the audience, and the scene plays as slow. If the audience must already know, restructure so the drama is the *listener's* reaction, and shorten the speech accordingly.
**Example:**
> "I didn't go back for the keys. I want to say I went back for the keys."
> *Beat.*
> "I went back because I wanted to see if he was still breathing. And he was."

**Yields to:** `info.reveal_lands_on_character` — Audience already knows it; play the listener.  
`dial.confession_speech`

### The Toast

**Also called:** the wedding speech, public praise
**What it is:** A speech delivered to a room on a happy occasion, in which the speaker's private situation leaks through the public form.
**Effect on the audience:** Sustained dread or sustained ache, depending on genre, because a toast is the one speech that cannot be stopped and cannot be honest. Everyone present is obliged to smile at it.
**Used for and where it works best:** The single most efficient ensemble device in dialogue, because it puts every character in one room, gives one of them the floor by right, and forbids all the others from responding. Write it in two channels: the correct public speech, and the specific detail that only three people in the room can decode. The decoding characters must be on camera. The classic structure is praise, anecdote, praise — and the anecdote is where the leak happens.
**Best in:** formats: Feature Film, One-Hour Drama, Stage Play, Limited Series, Short Film, Novel | genres: Family Drama, Drama, Comedy, Social Drama, Tragedy, Satire, Heritage
**Avoid when:** The audience does not know the private situation, or does not know who in the room knows it. A toast with no second channel is a wedding video. Also avoid the speaker breaking down and saying the true thing aloud — the whole power is that they do not, and cannot.
**Example:**
> "To my brother. Who taught me that when you want something, you take it before somebody else does."
> *Laughter. His wife does not laugh.*
> "He'll tell you he's changed. To Sami."

**Yields to:** `dial.confession_speech` — The true thing must be said aloud.  
`dial.the_toast`

### The Pitch

**Also called:** the sell, the persuasion speech
**What it is:** A character verbally sells something — an idea, a plan, themselves — to a listener with the power to refuse, in a speech whose shape is designed to close.
**Effect on the audience:** Active judgement. A pitch is the only speech form where the audience naturally scores each line, because they are deciding alongside the listener.
**Used for and where it works best:** Anywhere a character's competence needs demonstrating in one scene: the con, the job interview, the proposal to the board, the recruiter, the seduction. The rule that makes it dramatic rather than informative is that the listener must visibly move — resist, soften, resist again — so the pitch is being re-aimed in real time. A pitch delivered straight through to a stone face is a speech about the plot. The strongest version has the speaker abandon the prepared pitch halfway and improvise the true one.
**Best in:** formats: Feature Film, One-Hour Drama, Half-Hour Comedy, Limited Series, Stage Play, Game Narrative, Podcast | genres: Crime, Political, Comedy, Drama, Thriller, Satire, Social Drama, Noir
**Avoid when:** The audience already knows the answer is no. Then the pitch is an execution and should be cut to its first and last lines. Also avoid the pitch that is secretly exposition — if the listener would not need those facts, neither does the scene.
**Example:**
> "Three floors, forty rooms, and the licence is already —"
> *She is looking at her watch.*
> "You're not going to buy it. I know. I came so I could say I asked."
> *She stops looking at her watch.*

**Yields to:** `dial.enter_late_leave_early` — Answer is already no; cut to first and last lines.  
`dial.the_pitch`

### The Eulogy

**Also called:** the graveside speech, speaking for the dead
**What it is:** A speech about someone absent and unable to answer, delivered publicly, in which the speaker's relationship to the dead is exposed by what they choose to say and what they leave out.
**Effect on the audience:** Grief they arrive at sideways. A eulogy that states the loss produces nothing; one that describes a habit, a smell or a small argument produces everything.
**Used for and where it works best:** Endings, and mid-story deaths that must re-aim the survivors. Write it as a list of specifics with no adjectives of feeling in it — what he kept in the car, what she said about the neighbours — and let one specific be slightly wrong, so another character's face carries the correction. It is also the most reliable way to characterise a dead person the audience barely met, which is a problem most scripts solve badly. Cross-reference `emo.specific_detail` and `emo.understate_at_peak`.
**Best in:** formats: Feature Film, One-Hour Drama, Novel, Stage Play, Short Film, Limited Series, Documentary | genres: Drama, Family Drama, Tragedy, War, Heritage, Social Drama, Coming of Age
**Avoid when:** The speech is being used to summarise the dead character's function in the plot. That is a recap in black clothes and every audience recognises it. Also avoid the eulogy that forgives — if the story has not resolved the grievance, the speech must not either.
**Example:**
> "He never once let anyone else drive. Not my mother, not me, not when his eyes went."
> *Pause.*
> "The car's still outside. I don't know what we're supposed to do about the car."

`dial.the_eulogy`

### The Shape of a Rant

**Also called:** the tirade, the escalating complaint
**What it is:** A speech of sustained anger built as a rising structure — a small specific grievance, widening to a larger one, arriving at the real one — rather than as a flat block of shouting.
**Effect on the audience:** Exhilaration if the shape is right, embarrassment if it is not. A rant is the closest dialogue comes to music, and it fails on rhythm rather than on content.
**Used for and where it works best:** The rules are structural. Start small and concrete: never open a rant on the big grievance, because there is nowhere to go. Accelerate by shortening sentences, not by adding volume. Put one moment of derailment in it, where the speaker loses their thread and recovers, which is the only thing that makes it sound unwritten. And land on the real subject, which the speaker did not intend to reach — the rant should surprise the person giving it. Comedy and drama use the identical structure; only the last line differs.
**Best in:** formats: Stage Play, Feature Film, Half-Hour Comedy, One-Hour Drama, Podcast, Novel, Audio Drama | genres: Comedy, Drama, Social Drama, Political, Satire, Family Drama, Tragedy
**Avoid when:** The character is powerful. A rant is what people do when they have no other instrument, so giving one to a character who could simply act instead makes them smaller — which may be what you want, but it is a decision, not a default. Also avoid two rants in one work by the same character; the second one is noise.
**Example:**
> "The bin. Two weeks, the bin, right there, with the lid open."
> "It's a bin."
> "And the window, and the tap that nobody, and the — do you know I asked you in March? March. I have asked you every month since March, and you say Friday, you have said Friday nine times, and I am not — "
> *She stops.*
> "I am not going to be the person who counts. I don't want to be the person who counts."

**Yields to:** `dial.polite_aggression` — The speaker holds power and could simply act.  
`dial.rant_shape`

---

## Group and ensemble scenes

### The Three-Hander

**Also called:** the triangle scene, three in the room
**What it is:** A scene built for exactly three speakers, where the drama comes from the shifting two-against-one that three people cannot avoid forming.
**Effect on the audience:** Constant low-level suspense about alignment. With two people the audience watches a contest; with three they watch a vote.
**Used for and where it works best:** The most under-used scene shape in dialogue, and the fix for a two-hander that has run out of moves. The craft rule is that the coalition must change at least once inside the scene, and the moment it changes is the scene's turn. Give each character a different relationship to the scene's question — one wants it settled, one wants it postponed, one wants it raised — rather than three positions on the same axis. The third character is never a witness; if they could leave without changing anything, write a two-hander. See `rel.triangle` and `rel.shifting_coalition`.
**Best in:** formats: Stage Play, Feature Film, One-Hour Drama, Limited Series, Novel, Short Film, Audio Drama | genres: Drama, Family Drama, Crime, Social Drama, Tragedy, Psychological, Political
**Avoid when:** Two of the three want identical things and one is merely support. That is a two-hander with an audience member in it, and the extra body slows every exchange without adding a move.
**Example:**
> "We're selling it."
> "We haven't agreed that."
> "Layla?"
> *Layla says nothing.*
> "Layla."
> "I think we should hear what the offer is."
> *— and it is now two against one, and it was not a minute ago.*

**Yields to:** `scene.two_hander` — The third has nothing to want.  
`dial.three_hander`

### The Table Scene

**Also called:** the dinner scene, the seated ensemble
**What it is:** A long scene with the whole cast seated and unable to leave, in which the social form of the meal — serving, passing, eating, refusing food — carries the conflict that the dialogue cannot state.
**Effect on the audience:** Claustrophobia and anticipation. The audience knows something will be said and knows nobody can walk out before it is.
**Used for and where it works best:** The best available container for family drama, and for heritage work where the food itself carries the world. Four things make it work. Seat people deliberately, and make the seating a decision someone made. Give the scene a physical clock — a dish that will be served, a course that ends it. Run at least two conversations at the table, so attention can cut. And give the explosive line to the person nobody has been watching. Pair with `dial.overlap` from Part 1 for texture and `dial.talking_to_the_room` for the weapon.
**Best in:** formats: Feature Film, One-Hour Drama, Stage Play, Limited Series, Novel, Short Film | genres: Family Drama, Drama, Social Drama, Heritage, Tragedy, Comedy, Historical
**Avoid when:** The cast is above about seven and the audience does not yet know them. A table of strangers is a wall of names, and the audience spends the scene doing identification instead of watching. Introduce the room in pairs first — `rel.pair_off_the_room` — then seat them.
**Example:**
> "Pass the bread to your uncle."
> "He has bread."
> "Pass it anyway."
> *He passes it. His uncle does not take it.*

**Yields to:** `rel.pair_off_the_room` — Cast above seven and still unknown.  
`dial.table_scene`

### Who Is Silent

**Also called:** the non-speaker, the watching character
**What it is:** A deliberate decision to keep one character in a group scene entirely without lines, and to place the camera or the prose attention on them at chosen moments.
**Effect on the audience:** They align with the silent one. Attention goes to the person not competing for it, and the audience adopts that character's reading of the room.
**Used for and where it works best:** Any scene above three speakers, and it should be decided before the scene is written rather than discovered after. The silent character must have a *reason* — outranked, guilty, new, or holding the information everyone else lacks — and they must be given two or three physical moments so the audience knows their silence is being tracked. The payoff is the first line they speak, which should end the scene. Cross-reference `rel.ensemble_scene_legibility`.
**Best in:** formats: Feature Film, One-Hour Drama, Stage Play, Limited Series, Novel, Short Film, Comics | genres: Drama, Family Drama, Crime, War, Social Drama, Psychological, Tragedy
**Avoid when:** The format cannot show them. Audio drama and podcast cannot hold a silent character — with no image they simply cease to exist for the listener — so an audio ensemble needs everyone to speak at intervals or to be verbally referred to. This is the sharpest formal limit in ensemble dialogue.
**Example:**
> *Four people arguing about the sale. Fifth, at the end of the table, eats.*
> *He puts down the fork.*
> "It's not ours to sell."

**Yields to:** `dial.spoken_about_present` — Audio: a silent character must be referred to aloud.  
`dial.who_is_silent`

### Spoken About While Present

**Also called:** the third person in the room, discussed in front of
**What it is:** Two or more characters discuss a person who is present, referring to them in the third person, as though they were absent or incapable.
**Effect on the audience:** Precise humiliation, and in comedy, precise absurdity. The audience feels the erasure because they can see the erased person's face.
**Used for and where it works best:** The most efficient way to dramatise power over a person rather than over a situation — medicine, custody, migration, elder care, disability, any institution meeting a family. It is distinct from `dial.talking_to_the_room` in Part 1, where a character is a delivery mechanism; here they are the *subject* and still not addressed. The rule: the discussed character must attempt to enter the conversation once and be overridden, or the audience reads them as absent rather than excluded.
**Best in:** formats: Feature Film, One-Hour Drama, Stage Play, Short Film, Novel, Limited Series, Documentary | genres: Social Drama, Family Drama, Drama, Tragedy, Satire, Political, Coming of Age
**Avoid when:** It is used for pity alone. The technique is strongest when the discussed character is competent and the room is wrong, and it becomes sentimental the moment they are merely a victim. Give them the last line of the scene, or do not use it.
**Example:**
> "Does she manage the stairs at home?"
> "I manage the stairs."
> "She has trouble in the mornings, doctor."
> "I manage the stairs."

**Yields to:** `dial.talking_to_the_room` — The present person is a conduit, not the subject.  
`dial.spoken_about_present`

### Everyone Gets a Line

**Also called:** the democratic scene, round-robin dialogue
**This is a named failure, not a recommendation.**
**What it is:** In a group scene, every character is given roughly equal speaking time so that none is neglected — usually out of loyalty to the cast rather than to the scene.
**Effect on the audience:** A scene with no shape. Attention has nowhere to settle, no coalition forms, and the audience cannot tell whose scene it is — which means they cannot tell what it was about.
**Used for and where it works best:** One legitimate cousin, and it is a different thing wearing the same shape: the deliberate round of ritual speech — a briefing where each person reports, an oath taken in turn, a vote counted aloud — where the equality of the turns is itself the content and the tension is in whose turn is coming.
**Best in:** formats: — | genres: —
**Avoid when:** Always, in dramatic scenes. The fix is structural, not verbal: decide before writing whose scene it is, give that character roughly half the lines, give one antagonist most of the rest, and let two or three people contribute a line each or none at all. Across an episode the spotlight rotates — `rel.rotating_spotlight` — but inside a scene it does not. A cast member with nothing to want in this scene should be silent in it, which is `dial.who_is_silent` and is a better use of them anyway — except in audio drama and podcast, where a silent character ceases to exist; there that card's own limit holds and they speak at intervals or are referred to aloud (`dial.spoken_about_present`).
**Example:**
> **Failure:** six characters, six roughly equal speeches, all agreeing with variation.
> **Working:** one character pushing, one refusing, one switching sides, three silent — and the switch is the scene.

**Yields to:** `dial.who_is_silent` — Give the uninterested cast member silence, not a line.  
`dial.everyone_gets_a_line`

---

## Telephone and mediated conversation

### The One-Sided Call

**Also called:** the half conversation, hearing one end
**What it is:** Only one participant in a call is seen and heard. The other end is inferred entirely from pauses, responses and the visible character's reactions.
**Effect on the audience:** Active reconstruction, which is engagement. They assemble the missing half themselves and are more convinced by it than by anything you could have written.
**Used for and where it works best:** Any call where the *reaction* matters more than the content — bad news, a refusal, a demand. It is also the cheapest scene in production and the most performable, which is why it is standard in short film and micro-drama. Two craft rules. Never have the character repeat the other end back ("You're saying the results came back positive?") — that is `dial.known_information` wearing a telephone. And write the pauses as beats of specific action, so the actor has a length to play.
**Best in:** formats: Short Film, Feature Film, Vertical Micro-Drama, One-Hour Drama, Reels/Shorts, Stage Play, Novel | genres: Drama, Thriller, Crime, Family Drama, Psychological, Noir, Romance
**Avoid when:** The audience needs the other end's exact words for the plot. Inference is approximate, and a plot point delivered by inference will be missed by a third of the audience. Also avoid in audio-only formats, where a one-sided call is indistinguishable from a monologue.
**Example:**
> "Yes."
> *She sits down on the arm of the chair.*
> "How long has he — no. No, I'd rather you didn't."
> *She picks a thread off her sleeve.*
> "Tell him I'll come Thursday."

**Yields to:** `dial.voice_note` — Audio-only: a half-call is indistinguishable from monologue.  
`dial.one_sided_call`

### The Intercut Call

**Also called:** both ends, cross-cut conversation
**What it is:** Both parties to a call are seen, cutting between two locations, so the audience holds two rooms at once during a single conversation.
**Effect on the audience:** Dramatic irony as standard equipment. Each character speaks without knowing what the other's room contains, and the audience knows both.
**Used for and where it works best:** Whenever the *contrast between the two spaces* is the point — one calm room and one on fire, one person lying and one surrounded by the evidence of the lie. Load the second location with one visual fact that contradicts what that character is saying, and hold on it. The rule that keeps it from going slack: the two rooms must be on different clocks, so cutting away creates a cost. Pairs with `info.dramatic_irony`.
**Best in:** formats: Feature Film, One-Hour Drama, Limited Series, Vertical Micro-Drama, Animation Feature, Comics | genres: Thriller, Crime, Drama, Family Drama, Romance, Political, Noir
**Avoid when:** The second location adds nothing. Cutting to a person standing in a neutral room holding a phone halves the tension of the scene you had and buys nothing — that call should be one-sided. Also expensive in production terms for a gain that is often decorative.
**Example:**
> **HER (kitchen):** "Are you still at the office?"
> **HIM (car, engine off, outside a house that is not his):** "Just finishing up."
> **HER:** "I can hear the indicator."
> **HIM:** *He turns it off.* "That's the printer."

**Yields to:** `dial.one_sided_call` — The second location adds nothing.  
`dial.intercut_call`

### Text on Screen

**Also called:** displayed messages, on-screen text bubbles
**What it is:** Written messages between characters rendered visually — as floating text, phone screens, or typed-and-deleted drafts — rather than spoken.
**Effect on the audience:** A different register entirely from speech: flatter, more deniable, and readable more than once. Text is the only dialogue form where the audience watches a line being composed.
**Used for and where it works best:** The typing indicator and the deleted draft are the two things this form can do that speech cannot, and they are the whole reason to use it — a message written, revised and not sent is a confession the character never made. Keep messages to a few words; long text on screen becomes reading homework and the audience's eye leaves the actor's face. In vertical formats it is native and needs no framing device. Cross-reference `expo.diegetic_text`.
**Best in:** formats: Vertical Micro-Drama, Reels/Shorts, Feature Film, One-Hour Drama, Limited Series, Comics, Game Narrative | genres: Romance, Thriller, Coming of Age, Drama, Crime, Psychological, Social Drama
**Avoid when:** The project will be subtitled or dubbed. Burned-in on-screen text collides with the subtitle band, and localising it means re-rendering every graphic — a real budget line that kills the technique on low-cost multilingual work. Also avoid where the emotional content needs a voice; text strips tone deliberately, so it cannot carry a scene that must be warm.
**Shelf life:** dated — review 2027-09. Rests on 2026 platform and caption conventions.
**Example:**
> **typing…**
> **typing…**
> *The indicator stops. Nothing arrives.*
> **HER:** "ok"

**Yields to:** `dial.voice_note` — Localisation cost, or the scene must be warm.  
`dial.text_on_screen`

### The Voice Note

**Also called:** the recorded message, the asynchronous speech
**What it is:** A character speaks into a recording — voicemail, voice note, a message they may or may not send — addressed to someone who is not present and cannot interrupt.
**Effect on the audience:** Unusual intimacy. The speaker is performing for one listener and the audience is over that listener's shoulder, which is closer than either monologue or conversation.
**Used for and where it works best:** The one form that legitimately allows an uninterrupted speech in a modern setting without violating `dial.interrupted_monologue` — the format supplies the reason nobody speaks back. Strongest when it is unheard: the note recorded and deleted, the voicemail left for someone who is dead, the message played months later in a different context. It is also the standard way to deliver a confession in audio formats, where no other private-speech convention exists. Keep the false starts in; a voice note with no restart sounds written.
**Best in:** formats: Audio Drama, Podcast, Feature Film, Vertical Micro-Drama, Short Film, One-Hour Drama, Novel | genres: Drama, Romance, Crime, Psychological, Family Drama, Thriller, Coming of Age
**Avoid when:** It is being used to deliver plot the character has no reason to record. A voice note that explains the situation to someone who lived it is `dial.known_information` with a timestamp — and the timestamp makes it worse, because the audience can see the character choosing to say it.
**Example:**
> "It's me. It's — you know it's me, your phone says."
> *Pause.*
> "I'm not going to come on Sunday. That's all. That's the whole — "
> *Pause.*
> "Delete this."

`dial.voice_note`

### The Video Call

**Also called:** the framed conversation, screen-to-screen
**What it is:** A conversation conducted through cameras, where each character controls what their own frame shows and the audience sees both the frame and, sometimes, what is outside it.
**Effect on the audience:** Suspicion. A video call is a scene in which both people are lying about their surroundings by default, and the audience is trained to look at the edges.
**Used for and where it works best:** Anywhere concealment is spatial rather than verbal — who else is in the room, where the character actually is, what is on the wall behind them. The craft move is to show the audience one character's full room and only the other's frame, which creates asymmetry without a word. Also a genuine solution for long-distance relationships, prison and migration stories, where the call is the whole relationship and its poverty is the subject. The eye-contact problem is a gift: two people on a video call are never quite looking at each other, and that is worth writing into the scene.
**Best in:** formats: Feature Film, One-Hour Drama, Limited Series, Vertical Micro-Drama, Short Film, Game Narrative | genres: Thriller, Drama, Romance, Social Drama, Psychological, Crime, Family Drama
**Avoid when:** The scene is long. Screen-mediated staging flattens fast — the compositions repeat and the actors cannot touch anything — so past about three pages it becomes visually inert regardless of how good the dialogue is. Cut away, or bring them into a room.
**Example:**
> "Turn the camera round. Show me the room."
> "It's a mess."
> "Show me the room, Marwan."
> *He turns it. The room is empty. He turns it back too quickly.*

**Yields to:** `dial.intercut_call` — Past about three pages the framed staging goes inert.  
`dial.video_call`

### Lag as Drama

**Also called:** latency, the delay, the transmission gap
**What it is:** The technical delay in a mediated conversation — a bad line, a satellite hop, a translation relay, a spacecraft — made into the scene's central tension rather than a nuisance to be smoothed over.
**Effect on the audience:** Unbearable waiting, felt in the body. Every delay is a small suspense, and the audience experiences the gap at the same length the character does, which almost nothing else in dialogue achieves.
**Used for and where it works best:** Scenes where the delay makes an answer arrive too late to help: a decision being made while the advice is still travelling, an apology crossing a refusal in transit. Write the overlap explicitly — both characters speaking into the gap, each responding to a line the other has already abandoned. In audio formats this is unusually strong, because the silence is the only thing in the medium. Note that `dial.overlap` in Part 1 is the opposite failure mode of the same social machinery.
**Best in:** formats: Audio Drama, Feature Film, Podcast, One-Hour Drama, Limited Series, Game Narrative, Short Film | genres: Thriller, War, Drama, Psychological, Romance, Social Drama
**Avoid when:** The delay is short enough to read as bad editing. Under about two seconds the audience blames the sound mix, not the satellite, so the gap must be long and established early — show a first exchange where the delay is harmless and explained, then use it when it costs something.
**Example:**
> "Don't sign anything until I— "
> *Four seconds.*
> "— sorry, say again?"
> "Don't sign it."
> *Four seconds.*
> "It's done. I signed it while you were talking."

`dial.lag_as_drama`

## Translated and bilingual dialogue

### Code-Switch Mid-Line

**Also called:** switching inside the sentence, intrasentential switching
**What it is:** A bilingual character changes language partway through a single line, usually on a specific word or a specific addressee, and switches back.
**Effect on the audience:** Precise social information. The switch marks exactly which part of the sentence belongs to which world — the private word, the word that has no equivalent, the word said so a child will not understand it.
**Used for and where it works best:** Diaspora and migrant stories, and any household running two languages, where this is simply accurate rather than decorative. Switch on meaning, not at random: the reliable triggers are emotion, family terms, food, prayer, insult, numbers and anything learned before the second language was. The craft rule is that the switch must be legible without translation — build the sentence so the surrounding language carries the meaning, and the switched word carries the temperature. See `voice.code_switching` for the narrative-voice version and `sub.across_languages` for the subtext layer.
**Best in:** formats: Feature Film, One-Hour Drama, Novel, Limited Series, Stage Play, Short Film, Vertical Micro-Drama | genres: Family Drama, Social Drama, Drama, Coming of Age, Heritage, Comedy, Romance
**Avoid when:** The switching is sprinkled for flavour by a writer who does not speak the language. Bilingual audiences detect wrong switch points instantly — not wrong words, wrong *points* — and the character is finished for exactly the viewers the choice was meant to serve.
**Example:**
> "He said he'd pay by Friday, and I said fine, ya ammi, fine, take your time — *he has had six months.*"

**Yields to:** `dial.second_language_rhythm` — Writer cannot place switch points credibly.  
`dial.code_switch_midline`

### The Untranslated Line

**Also called:** the unsubtitled moment, withheld translation
**What it is:** A line spoken in another language and deliberately left without subtitles, so that one part of the audience understands it and the rest is placed in the position of the character who does not.
**Effect on the audience:** Split. The bilingual viewer receives a private gift; the monolingual viewer receives the exclusion that is the scene's actual subject. Both are correct readings and that is the design.
**Used for and where it works best:** Occupation, migration, interrogation and any scene about being outside the language. Rules: use it where the *content* is not required, only the exclusion — never on plot. Keep it short, because untranslated speech past a few seconds reads as a technical fault. And put the excluded character on screen so the audience has someone to be stranded with. The reverse also works: subtitle everything except one line, and the omission becomes the loudest thing in the scene.
**Best in:** formats: Feature Film, Limited Series, One-Hour Drama, Short Film, Documentary, Stage Play | genres: War, Social Drama, Political, Drama, Heritage, Thriller, Historical
**Avoid when:** Distribution will not permit it. Many platforms mandate full subtitling for accessibility compliance, and an accessibility pass will translate your deliberate omission and delete the technique without telling you. If you need it, flag it in the delivery notes as a creative forced-narrative decision, in writing, early.
**Shelf life:** dated — review 2027-09. Rests on 2026 distribution and subtitling practice.
**Example:**
> **SOLDIER:** *(in Arabic, unsubtitled)* "ابنك مو هنا. روح للبيت."
> **THE MOTHER:** "I don't— what is he saying? What is he saying to me?"

**Yields to:** `dial.interpreter_scene` — Platform mandates full subtitles; stage exclusion through the relay.  
`dial.untranslated_line`

### Fluency That Moves with Stress

**Also called:** the receding second language, fluency under load
**What it is:** A character's command of their second language rises and falls with their emotional state — fluent when calm or professional, collapsing into first-language syntax, then into the first language entirely, under fear, rage, exhaustion or pain.
**Effect on the audience:** A live readout of the character's internal state, requiring no description at all. When the grammar goes, the audience knows before the character does.
**Used for and where it works best:** The single best technique available for bilingual characters, and badly under-used. Establish the fluent baseline in two early scenes so the collapse is measurable. Stage it in three steps rather than one: idiom goes first, then articles and tense, then the language itself. Reverse it for a different effect — a character who becomes *more* formal and more correct under stress is holding themselves together, which is a different person entirely. The classic placement is that a character curses, prays and counts in their first language whatever their fluency.
**Best in:** formats: Feature Film, One-Hour Drama, Novel, Limited Series, Stage Play, Short Film, Audio Drama | genres: War, Social Drama, Drama, Thriller, Family Drama, Psychological, Coming of Age
**Avoid when:** The audience has only met the character under stress. With no fluent baseline the collapse reads as the character's normal state, and you have written a stereotype instead of an arc. Two calm scenes first, minimum.
**Example:**
> **Scene 4:** "I appreciate your time. I'll have the documents to you by Tuesday."
> **Scene 30:** "No. No, you listen — is my son, this is my son, why you are — "
> *She stops. She says the rest to the floor, in Assyrian, and nobody translates it.*

**Yields to:** `dial.second_language_rhythm` — No room to establish a fluent baseline.  
`dial.fluency_under_stress`

### Writing for the Subtitle

**Also called:** the two-line constraint, subtitle-aware dialogue
**What it is:** Writing dialogue with the knowledge that it will be read rather than heard by part of the audience, and shaping line length, wordplay and overlap around what a subtitle can physically carry.
**Effect on the audience:** In the target language, a scene that plays at the speed it was written. Without it, the translated audience receives a compressed summary and blames the actors.
**Used for and where it works best:** Any project intended to travel, and mandatory for work that ships with burned-in subtitles where nothing can be fixed later. The practical constraints: roughly two lines, each within the destination's line length (`dubbing.subtitle_vs_spoken_rate`), on screen long enough to read at the rate `tens.subtitle_preempt` gives — which in practice means a line lasting under about one second cannot be subtitled at all. Consequences for the writing: no two characters speaking at once on plot, no joke whose punch depends on a word arriving last if the target language reorders, and no rapid volley of one-word lines. Where the work is heavily verbal, buy the speed back with `dial.job_syntax` and behaviour. See `rhythm.subtitle_beat` and `comedy.translation_resistance`.
**Best in:** formats: Feature Film, Documentary, Limited Series, Reels/Shorts, Vertical Micro-Drama, One-Hour Drama, Animation Feature | genres: Heritage, Historical, Social Drama, Drama, Political, War, Thriller
**Avoid when:** The work is monolingual by design and the constraint would flatten the writing — a stage play, a domestic-market comedy built on overlapping speed. Do not pre-shrink dialogue for a translation that is not coming; that is a real cost paid for a hypothetical benefit.
**Source:** assumption — the line figures are rounded from `dubbing.subtitle_vs_spoken_rate`, which owns them; the claim that a line under about one second cannot be subtitled is this card's own estimate, untested
**Shelf life:** dated — review 2027-09. Character-per-line and reading-rate limits are current platform specs, not craft.
**Example:**
> **Untranslatable:** "You said you'd handle it — " "I did handle it — " "You handled it like you handle everything — " "Meaning?" "Meaning."
> **Subtitle-safe:** "You said you'd handle it."
> "I did."
> "The way you handle everything."

**Yields to:** `dial.overlap` — Monolingual by design; do not pre-shrink the speed.  
`dial.subtitle_constraint`

### The Interpreter in the Scene

**Also called:** the third voice, mediated translation
**What it is:** A scene in which two characters cannot speak to each other directly and a third person converts between them — a professional interpreter, a bilingual child, a soldier, a relative.
**Effect on the audience:** Triple attention. They watch the speaker, the interpreter's choices, and the listener's reaction to a version they cannot check.
**Used for and where it works best:** Immigration, medicine, courts, war, and family scenes where a child interprets for a parent — which is the most loaded version, because it inverts the household's power for the length of the scene. The drama lives entirely in the gap between what is said and what is relayed: softening, shortening, editorialising, refusing. Give the audience the true version — subtitled or previously known — so they can hear what the interpreter did to it. The interpreter is never neutral and should never be written as a device. Cross-reference `dial.deflection` and `char.status_flip`.
**Best in:** formats: Feature Film, One-Hour Drama, Stage Play, Limited Series, Short Film, Documentary, Novel | genres: Social Drama, War, Political, Family Drama, Drama, Crime, Coming of Age
**Avoid when:** The scene is on a clock. Interpreted dialogue runs at roughly half speed because everything is said twice, so it cannot carry a chase, an argument at pace or a short-form scene. Budget the runtime honestly before you commit to the staging.
**Example:**
> **DOCTOR:** "We need to talk about what happens if the treatment doesn't work."
> **THE SON, to his mother, in Arabic:** "He says the medicine is good and we will see in one month."
> **THE MOTHER:** *(in Arabic)* "Why is he looking at me like that?"
> **THE SON, to the doctor:** "She says thank you."

**Yields to:** `dial.untranslated_line` — The scene is on a clock.  
`dial.interpreter_scene`

## Coverage

Four cards are named failures rather than recommendations: `dial.phonetic_accent_spelling`, `dial.writer_voice_uniformity`, `dial.talking_past_the_laugh` and `dial.everyone_gets_a_line`. One card is explicitly perishable — `dial.generational_speech` — because current slang dates faster than any other element in this category; everything else here is durable craft. Three cards carry live 2026 distribution constraints rather than craft rules: `dial.untranslated_line` (platform accessibility mandates), `dial.text_on_screen` (localisation cost) and `dial.subtitle_constraint` (character and timing limits).

*Build notes from when this file was drafted — targets, running totals and what remained to be written — are kept verbatim in the [coverage history](../tools/history/coverage-history.md). They were true of the draft, not of the file, so they no longer sit here as if they were measurements.*
